title: Recognising postoperative complications
blurb: Spot bleeding, hypothermia, low urine output, wound infection, VTE risk and delirium after surgery, and act on each.
question: Mr Clarke, 69, returned from a hip replacement 4 hours ago. His pulse has risen from 78 to 112, his BP has fallen from 132/80 to 104/66, his hands are cool and his urine output is 20 mL in the last hour. What is the most appropriate action?

teach.body: A postoperative complication is any harmful event that follows surgery: bleeding and hypovolaemic shock, inadvertent hypothermia, urinary retention and acute kidney injury, chest complications, venous thromboembolism, surgical site infection and delirium. Plain English: the operation is over, but the body is still under stress. The nurse's job is to notice the early, quiet changes (a rising pulse, a falling urine output, a cooler patient, a muddled answer) before they become an emergency, and to escalate using NEWS2.
teach.cite: NICE CG50 (track and trigger for all adults); NICE CG65, NG125, NG148, NG89, CG103

head: Complication
Early clue
First response
teach.caption: Each line is covered below. Use NEWS2 for every set of observations (CG50).

steps.label: Act now
steps.sub: Escalate, check wound and drains, fluids as prescribed

teach.caption: NICE CG174 indicators for urgent fluid resuscitation include systolic BP below 100, HR above 90, capillary refill over 2 seconds or cold peripheries, RR above 20 and NEWS 5 or more.
Normothermia is 36.5–37.5 °C. In recovery: temperature every 15 minutes, forced-air warming if below 36.0 °C, ward transfer once 36.0 °C or above.

items: Recovery: measure on arrival and every 15 minutes.
Below 36.0 °C: forced-air warming until discharged from recovery or comfortably warm; do not arrange ward transfer until 36.0 °C or above.
Ward: measure on arrival, then with routine 4-hourly observations; at least 1 cotton sheet plus 2 blankets, or a duvet.
Falls below 36.0 °C on the ward: forced-air warming, temperature at least every 30 minutes while warming.

teach.body: NICE NG148 defines acute kidney injury in adults by a creatinine rise of 26 micromol/L or more within 48 hours, a 50% or greater rise within 7 days, or urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/hour for more than 6 hours. After surgery, keep an accurate fluid balance, dipstick the urine when AKI is suspected, and flag nephrotoxic medicines such as NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs and diuretics. A palpable, tender bladder with little urine suggests retention, a different and fixable cause.

children.label: May shower; tap water if wound separated or opened

teach.caption: Do not use topical antimicrobials on wounds healing by primary intention; do not use Eusol and gauze or moist cotton gauze for wounds healing by secondary intention.

teach.text: A falling blood pressure is a LATE sign of bleeding. Do not wait for hypotension: a rising pulse, cool peripheries and falling urine output in a fresh postoperative patient need escalating now. And new drowsiness after surgery is not 'tiredness': hypoactive delirium is easily missed.

teach.h: Scenario: Mr Clarke after hip replacement
teach.body: Mr Clarke, 69, is 4 hours back from theatre. His pulse has climbed from 78 to 112, BP has fallen from 132/80 to 104/66, his hands are cool, capillary refill is 3 seconds and he passed 20 mL of urine in the last hour. The nurse recognises early hypovolaemia, escalates urgently using SBAR, checks the wound, dressing and drain for blood loss, and gives fluids as prescribed. Waiting for the next 4-hourly observations would be unsafe.

items.label: sterile saline, then the person may shower
urine output below this for 6 h = AKI
extended LMWH considered after major abdominal cancer surgery

teach.caption: CG65 rec 1.4.1; NG125 recs 1.4.2–1.4.4; NG148; NG89 (extended prophylaxis).

items: Rising pulse, cool peripheries and low urine output come before low BP: escalate early.
Recovery temperature every 15 minutes; forced-air warming below 36.0 °C; no ward transfer until 36.0 °C or above.
Sterile saline up to 48 hours; shower after 48 hours; antibiotic for suspected SSI with cellulitis.
AKI: urine below 0.5 mL/kg/h for over 6 hours or a creatinine rise; review nephrotoxic medicines.
New confusion or drowsiness after surgery: 4AT and look for the cause.

summary: You can now recognise the early signs of the common postoperative complications and choose the first nursing response for each. You can apply the NICE thresholds for temperature, wound cleansing and urine output to real patients.

A.q: Mr Lowe, 58, arrives in the recovery room after a 2-hour bowel operation with a temperature of 36.2 °C. How often should his temperature be measured and recorded while he is in recovery?
options: Every 15 minutes
Every 30 minutes
Every 60 minutes
Every 4 hours
A.why: NICE CG65 rec 1.4.1: measure and document temperature on admission to recovery and then every 15 minutes.

whyNot.1: Every 30 minutes is the intraoperative interval (and the ward interval during active warming).
whyNot.2: Hourly is too infrequent for recovery under CG65.
whyNot.3: 4-hourly is the routine ward interval once the patient is back on the ward.

A.q: Mr Evans, 80 kg, is on day 1 after a laparotomy. Which urine output, sustained for more than 6 hours, meets the NICE NG148 urine output criterion for acute kidney injury?
options: 50 mL per hour
45 mL per hour
30 mL per hour
40 mL per hour
A.why: The criterion is urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/hour for more than 6 hours. For 80 kg the cut-off is 40 mL/hour; 30 mL/hour is 0.375 mL/kg/hour, below it.

whyNot.0: 50 mL/hour is about 0.63 mL/kg/hour, above the threshold.
whyNot.1: 45 mL/hour is about 0.56 mL/kg/hour, above the threshold.
whyNot.3: 40 mL/hour is exactly 0.5 mL/kg/hour; the criterion is BELOW 0.5.

A.q: On day 1 after surgery, Mrs Shaw's routine 4-hourly temperature is 35.8 °C. According to NICE CG65, how should she be managed?
options: Extra blankets and a duvet, with temperature rechecked in 4 hours
Forced-air warming, with temperature at least every 30 minutes
Warmed IV fluids, with temperature rechecked in 1 hour
A warm drink, with temperature rechecked at the next round
A.why: CG65 rec 1.4.3: if temperature falls below 36.0 °C on the ward, warm with forced-air warming until comfortably warm and measure temperature at least every 30 minutes during warming.

whyNot.0: Blankets are the baseline for every patient; below 36.0 °C CG65 asks for forced-air warming and 30-minute checks.
whyNot.2: Warmed fluids are an intraoperative measure; the ward response is forced-air warming.
whyNot.3: A drink is not active warming, and waiting until the next round misses the 30-minute checks.

B.q: Mr Akhtar, 44, is on day 1 after an open appendicectomy. His dressing is soiled and needs changing. The wound edges are closed. How should the nurse clean and dress it?
options: Clean technique, cleansing with tap water
Aseptic non-touch technique, cleansing with sterile saline
Aseptic non-touch technique, then a topical antibiotic cream
Clean technique, leaving the wound uncleansed and redressed
B.why: NICE NG125 rec 1.4.1: use ANTT for changing surgical dressings; rec 1.4.2: sterile saline for wound cleansing up to 48 hours after surgery.

whyNot.0: Tap water is for after 48 hours, and only where the wound has separated or been opened; dressings need ANTT.
whyNot.2: Rec 1.4.5: do not use topical antimicrobial agents on wounds healing by primary intention.
whyNot.3: Dressing changes need ANTT, and a soiled wound in the first 48 hours is cleansed with sterile saline.

B.q: Mrs Doyle, 71, is on day 7 after a laparotomy. Part of her wound has been left open and is healing by secondary intention. Which approach to dressing it follows NICE NG125?
options: Eusol-soaked gauze changed twice daily
Moist cotton gauze packed loosely into the open wound cavity
Gauze soaked in a mercuric antiseptic solution
An interactive dressing, with tissue viability advice
B.why: NG125 recs 1.4.7–1.4.8: use an appropriate interactive dressing for wounds healing by secondary intention, and ask a tissue viability nurse for advice.

whyNot.0: Rec 1.4.6: do not use Eusol and gauze for wounds healing by secondary intention.
whyNot.1: Rec 1.4.6: moist cotton gauze is not recommended for these wounds.
whyNot.2: Rec 1.4.6: mercuric antiseptic solutions are not recommended.

B.q: Mr Clarke, 69, returned from a hip replacement 4 hours ago. Pulse has risen from 78 to 112, BP has fallen from 132/80 to 104/66, his hands are cool with a capillary refill of 3 seconds, and he passed 20 mL of urine in the last hour. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Recheck his observations at the next 4-hourly round
Give his oral analgesia, as pain explains the pulse
Escalate urgently and check the wound and drain for blood loss
Encourage oral fluids and review his urine output again in 2 hours
B.why: A rising pulse, cool peripheries, slow capillary refill and falling urine output soon after surgery suggest hypovolaemia from bleeding. These are CG174 indicators for urgent resuscitation, so escalate now and look for the source.

whyNot.0: Waiting 4 hours with signs of shock risks rapid deterioration; he needs escalation now.
whyNot.1: Pain can raise the pulse, but it does not explain cool peripheries, slow refill and low urine output together.
whyNot.3: Oral fluids will not correct possible bleeding, and a 2-hour wait delays treatment.

C.q: Mr Hassan, 78, is on day 2 after a bowel resection. Yesterday he was chatty; today he is drowsy, slow to answer and loses track of the conversation. His RR is 24, SpO2 93% on air and temperature 37.9 °C, with crackles at his right base. His daughter says, 'He's just tired after the operation.' What is the best response?
options: Agree that he needs rest and review him in the morning
Treat this as possible delirium from an acute cause and escalate
Reorientate him with a clock and recheck all his observations later
Ask his daughter to stay and keep him awake through the day
C.why: An acute change to drowsiness and inattention suggests hypoactive delirium (CG103), here with signs of a chest infection. Delirium is a sign of acute illness: escalate, assess with the 4AT and treat the underlying cause.

whyNot.0: Hypoactive delirium is easily mistaken for tiredness; delaying review misses a deteriorating patient.
whyNot.2: Reorientation helps, but it does not replace escalation when there are signs of infection and a new change in cognition.
whyNot.3: Family involvement supports care, but it does not deal with the likely chest infection behind the change.

C.q: Mr Ford, 72, is on day 1 after a laparotomy. He has peripheral arterial disease with weak foot pulses. His VTE prophylaxis plan includes LMWH and thigh-length anti-embolism stockings. What should the nurse do about the stockings?
options: Fit thigh-length stockings measured to his legs
Fit knee-length stockings instead, to reduce pressure on his feet
Withhold the stockings and ask for the plan to be reviewed
Fit them by day and remove them each night
C.why: NICE NG89 rec 1.3.1: do not offer anti-embolism stockings to people with suspected or proven peripheral arterial disease. The nurse withholds them and asks for the mechanical prophylaxis plan to be reviewed, while the LMWH continues as prescribed.

whyNot.0: Correct measuring matters, but stockings are contraindicated in peripheral arterial disease.
whyNot.1: Changing the length does not remove the contraindication.
whyNot.3: Partial wear does not make stockings safe in peripheral arterial disease; NICE says do not offer them.

C.q: Mr Evans, 80 kg, is on day 2 after a laparotomy. His urine output has been 25 mL/hour for 7 hours and his creatinine has risen from 90 to 122 micromol/L since yesterday. He takes regular paracetamol, ibuprofen, ondansetron and lactulose. Which medicine should the nurse raise first with the prescriber?
options: Regular paracetamol
Regular lactulose
Regular ondansetron
Regular ibuprofen
C.why: He meets NG148 AKI criteria (urine below 0.5 mL/kg/h for over 6 hours; creatinine rise of 26 micromol/L or more within 48 hours). NSAIDs such as ibuprofen are nephrotoxic and are listed as an AKI risk factor, so they should be reviewed first.

whyNot.0: Paracetamol is not a nephrotoxic drug in NG148 and remains part of multimodal analgesia.
whyNot.1: Lactulose is not a nephrotoxic medicine in NG148.
whyNot.2: Ondansetron is not one of the nephrotoxic medicines NG148 lists.

reteach.title: The body whispers before it shouts
reteach.question: Why does a careful nurse act on a rising pulse and a quiet, sleepy patient before the blood pressure falls?

blocks.body: After surgery the body defends its blood pressure by speeding the heart, narrowing vessels in the skin and saving water in the kidneys. So the early clues of bleeding are a faster pulse, cool skin and less urine, while the BP still looks acceptable. The brain is just as sensitive: new drowsiness or muddled answers may be delirium, a sign that something such as infection, low oxygen or low blood volume is wrong.

blocks.text: 'He's just tired after the operation' is the classic way hypoactive delirium is missed. A new change in alertness needs assessment, not rest.

explain.body: Watch the trend: pulse, capillary refill, urine output, then BP. CG174 lists systolic BP below 100, HR above 90, capillary refill over 2 seconds or cold peripheries, RR above 20 and NEWS 5 or more as indicators of need for urgent fluid resuscitation. Escalate, check wounds and drains, and give fluids as prescribed.

test.q: Which finding in a patient 3 hours after surgery is a CG174 indicator that urgent fluid resuscitation may be needed?
options: Capillary refill of 3 seconds
Respiratory rate of 18 per minute
Heart rate of 84
Systolic BP of 112
test.why: CG174 rec 1.2.1 includes capillary refill time over 2 seconds or cold peripheries among the indicators for urgent fluid resuscitation.

whyNot.1: The indicator is RR above 20; 18 is within it.
whyNot.2: The indicator is a heart rate above 90.
whyNot.3: The indicator is systolic BP below 100 mmHg.

explain.body: Normothermia is 36.5–37.5 °C. In recovery, temperature is checked every 15 minutes and anyone below 36.0 °C gets forced-air warming; ward transfer waits until 36.0 °C or above. On the ward, a fall below 36.0 °C means forced-air warming with checks at least every 30 minutes.

test.q: Mrs Rowe, 67, is ready to leave recovery but her temperature is 35.7 °C. What does NICE CG65 advise?
options: Transfer her with an extra blanket and recheck on the ward
Transfer her and start forced-air warming on the ward
Keep her in recovery, recheck in 1 hour and then transfer
Warm her with forced-air warming before arranging transfer
test.why: CG65 rec 1.4.1: ward transfer should not be arranged unless temperature is 36.0 °C or above; if below 36.0 °C, actively warm with forced-air warming.

whyNot.0: Transfer should not be arranged below 36.0 °C, and a blanket is not active warming.
whyNot.1: Warming should start in recovery, and transfer waits until she reaches 36.0 °C.
whyNot.2: She needs active forced-air warming now, not an hour's wait without warming.

explain.body: Use ANTT for dressings. Sterile saline cleanses the wound for the first 48 hours; after 48 hours the person may shower, and tap water is used if the wound has separated or been opened to drain pus. Suspected SSI with cellulitis needs an antibiotic covering likely organisms. Open wounds: interactive dressings and tissue viability advice.

test.q: Mr Patel is going home 24 hours after a laparoscopic hernia repair. He asks when he can shower. What should the nurse advise?
options: From 24 hours after surgery
From 48 hours after surgery
From 5 days after surgery
Once the stitches are removed
test.why: NICE NG125 rec 1.4.3: advise patients they may shower safely 48 hours after surgery.

whyNot.2: Five days is longer than NICE advises.
whyNot.3: NICE does not link showering to suture removal; it is safe from 48 hours.

explain.body: AKI: urine below 0.5 mL/kg/hour for more than 6 hours, or a creatinine rise of 26 micromol/L in 48 hours; review NSAIDs and other nephrotoxic drugs. VTE: follow the prophylaxis plan, mobilise early, and do not offer stockings with peripheral arterial disease. Delirium: new confusion or drowsiness needs a 4AT and a search for the cause.

test.q: Which creatinine change after surgery meets the NICE NG148 definition of acute kidney injury?
options: A rise of 20 micromol/L over 48 hours
A rise of 30% over 7 days
A rise of 30 micromol/L over 48 hours
A rise of 15 micromol/L over 24 hours
test.why: NG148: a rise in serum creatinine of 26 micromol/L or more within 48 hours meets the definition.

whyNot.0: 20 micromol/L is below the 26 micromol/L threshold.
whyNot.1: The 7-day criterion is a rise of 50% or more.
whyNot.3: 15 micromol/L is below the 26 micromol/L threshold.
